records.d: In the 1960s, TV weather presenters stood before blue screens while maps appeared behind them: reality edited live on broadcast. The background became replaceable. Live video learned to lie beautifully.
records.h: Chroma keyers replaced a color range with a second video feed in real time. The presenter pointed at nothing; viewers saw maps. The background was the first editable layer.
records.mj: Established - documented 1960s broadcast chroma key; live background replacement.
records.z: timeline|year=1965|span=1|events=chroma key weather broadcasts~live background replacement

records.d: The Scanimate, dominant in 1970s TV graphics, bent live video in real time: wobbling logos, flying text, analog effects. Video became malleable. The image could be played like an instrument.
records.h: Analog computers deflected the video raster to distort the picture live, with operators performing effects on knobs. The effect was the performance. Real-time video FX predated digital.
records.mj: Established - documented Scanimate analog video synthesis; real-time TV effects.
records.z: timeline|year=1973|span=1|events=Scanimate dominates TV graphics~analog real-time video FX

records.d: Photoshop 1.0, released in 1990, put professional image editing on the desktop: reality editable after the fact. The photograph stopped being evidence. Editing became a consumer skill.
records.h: Pixel-level tools, layers, and filters let users alter photographs convincingly. The undo button changed truth. Post-production editing went mainstream.
records.mj: Established - documented 1990 Photoshop 1.0; desktop image editing.

records.d: After Effects, launched in 1993, brought compositing to the desktop: layering, keying, and effects for video. Moving reality became editable. The music video learned new tricks.
records.h: Timeline-based compositing stacked video layers with effects and masks, rendered to tape. The desktop became a studio. Video post-production democratized.
records.mj: Established - documented 1993 After Effects; desktop video compositing.

records.d: Apple's Photo Booth, shipping in 2005, put live face effects on the webcam: distortions and backdrops in real time. The webcam became a toy. Consumers first edited their live image.
records.h: Real-time face detection drove distortion and backdrop effects on the live camera feed. The effect was instant. Live self-editing entered the home.
records.mj: Established - documented 2005 Photo Booth; live webcam effects.

records.d: Kinect, launched in November 2010, tracked bodies in 3D in real time: the player became the controller. Reality's geometry became input. The living room was scanned live.
records.h: Depth sensors and skeletal tracking mapped bodies at 30 fps, driving games without controllers. The body was the interface. Real-time 3D understanding of people went mass-market.
records.mj: Established - documented November 2010 launch; real-time body tracking.

records.d: Snapchat Lenses, launched in September 2015, put real-time face AR on hundreds of millions of phones: dog ears, flower crowns, face swaps. The selfie became editable live. AR went mainstream overnight.
records.h: Face-mesh tracking anchored 3D effects to facial landmarks at camera frame rates on phones. The filter was the message. Hundreds of millions edited their faces daily.
records.mj: Established - documented September 2015 launch; real-time face AR.

records.d: MSQRD's face-swap filters, acquired by a social media giant in 2016, made live face replacement a tap away. Your face became someone else's, live. Identity became a filter.
records.h: Real-time face mapping swapped facial features between people in the camera view. The swap was instant. The technology previewed deepfakes as consumer fun.
records.mj: Established - documented 2016 MSQRD acquisition; live face-swap filters.

records.d: Prisma, launched in June 2016, restyled photos as paintings with neural networks: your selfie as Van Gogh. AI edited aesthetics. The filter became an artist.
records.h: Neural style transfer applied artistic styles to photos via convolutional networks, first server-side then on-device. The aesthetic was computed. The photo became a painting.
records.mj: Established - documented June 2016 launch; neural style transfer app.

records.d: The iPhone X's TrueDepth camera, shipping in November 2017, mapped faces in 3D for Animoji: your expressions driving an animated character live. The face became a puppet controller. 3D self-tracking went pocket-sized.
records.h: Structured-light depth sensing built a 3D face mesh tracked in real time, driving avatar expressions. The puppet was your face. Consumer 3D face capture arrived.
records.mj: Established - documented November 2017 TrueDepth/Animoji; 3D face tracking.

records.d: In 2018, deepfakes emerged publicly: AI face-swaps in video, from entertainment to non-consensual abuse. Reality editing's dark side arrived with the technology. The same tool made fun and harm.
records.h: Autoencoder face-swap models trained on target faces produced convincing video replacements. Open-source tools spread. The technology forced the consent conversation.
records.mj: Established - documented 2018 deepfake emergence; AI face-swap technology.

records.d: In 2019, face-swap apps like Zao and Reface went viral: anyone's face in any video clip. Reality editing became a tap. The viral loop was identity play.
records.h: One-shot face-swap models inserted user faces into video templates in seconds. Sharing drove growth. The technology's fun side scaled.
records.mj: Established - documented 2019 viral face-swap apps; consumer face replacement.

records.d: In 2020, Zoom's virtual backgrounds became universal: living rooms replaced by beaches, offices, and memes. Reality editing entered work. The background became a choice.
records.h: Real-time segmentation separated people from backgrounds without green screens, compositing replacements live. The meeting was staged. Work's visual reality became editable.
records.mj: Established - documented 2020 adoption; real-time background replacement.

records.d: NVIDIA Broadcast, launched in 2020, used AI to remove backgrounds, noise, and echo from live streams: the stream cleaned itself. AI became the production crew. The bedroom became a studio.
records.h: GPU-accelerated models performed background removal, noise suppression, and auto-framing in real time. The software was the crew. Consumer streams gained broadcast polish.
records.mj: Established - documented 2020 NVIDIA Broadcast; AI live-stream enhancement.

records.d: By 2021, TikTok's effects were a creative medium: AR filters, greenscreen, and AI effects driving trends. The effect was the content. Reality editing became the art form.
records.h: An effects platform let creators build and share AR filters, with trends propagating through effect reuse. The filter was the meme. Editing tools became culture.
records.mj: Established - documented effects platform; AR effects driving trends.

records.d: By 2022, D-ID and peers were animating still photos into talking heads: portraits speaking on command. The photograph started talking. Still reality became live.
records.h: Image animation models drove facial motion from audio, making photos speak and emote. The portrait was the actor. The still image joined live media.
records.mj: Emerging - real products; photo-to-talking-head animation.

records.d: By 2023, generative fill reached video: AI extending, replacing, and altering footage from text prompts. The shot became editable by description. Post-production learned to imagine.
records.h: Video diffusion models inpainted and outpainted footage, replacing objects and extending scenes from prompts. The editor described; the AI rendered. The footage was clay.
records.mj: Emerging - real products; generative video fill and editing.
records.z: score|items=object replace:3:7~scene extend:3:7~temporal consistency:3:6|label=generative video fill

records.d: By 2023, Runway's tools were editing video with AI: style transfer, inpainting, and text-driven edits in the browser. The edit suite went neural. The timeline learned language.
records.h: Browser-based models applied AI edits to uploaded video: restyle, remove, generate. The suite was cloud. Editing became conversational.
records.mj: Emerging - real products; AI video editing suite.

records.d: OpenAI's Sora, announced in February 2024, generated minute-long photorealistic video from text: reality rendered from description. The camera became optional. Footage could be imagined.
records.h: Diffusion transformers modeled video at scale, generating coherent minute-long scenes from prompts. The footage never happened. The line between captured and created blurred.
records.mj: Emerging - real announced model (February 2024); text-to-video generation.

records.d: By 2024, live AI filters were transforming streams in real time: style transfer, avatar replacement, and scene edits on live video. The broadcast edited itself. Live gained post-production.
records.h: Real-time models applied transformations to live feeds at stream latency. The delay was the render. Live and edited merged.
records.mj: Emerging - real products; real-time AI live-video filters.

records.d: By 2025, real-time scene editing was reaching live production: virtual sets, object insertion, and relighting during broadcasts. The set became software. Live TV gained a render engine.
records.h: Game-engine virtual production plus AI relighting edited scenes live. The stage was computed. Broadcast and gaming pipelines merged.
records.mj: Emerging - real productions; real-time live scene editing.

records.d: By 2025, live AI dubbing with lip sync was translating streams in real time: speakers fluent in languages they never learned. The broadcast became polyglot. Language stopped being a barrier to liveness.
records.h: Speech translation plus visual lip-sync rendered translated speech matched to the speaker's mouth. The delay was seconds. The world watched together.
records.mj: Emerging - real products; live AI dubbing with lip sync.
